venue_now: not stated in the text; arXiv 2502.06453v2 [cs.LG], 12 Feb 2025 (p.1 stamp). No conference name appears in the extracted pages, so ICML 2025 cannot be confirmed from the text. Confirmed after the review: ICML 2025 poster on OpenReview (venue id ICML.cc/2025/Conference); Semantic Scholar also gives ICML (check_venues.py, notes/venue_check.json).
what_it_is: MATH-Perturb: 279 hand-written pairs of modifications of Level-5 (hardest) problems from the MATH dataset, one set of simple perturbations (MATH-P-Simple: non-essential changes, solvable by the same method, mostly numerical) and one of hard perturbations (MATH-P-Hard: small changes that make the original solution method inapplicable and need harder skills) (p.1-4). Twelve PhD-student annotators wrote them with minimal edits and a changed answer, and an independent annotator cross-validated each answer (p.3). Eighteen LLMs are scored on final-answer accuracy with zero-shot chain of thought and a SymPy-based equivalence check (p.4-5); all drop on MATH-P-Hard, and the authors trace many errors to a 'new form of memorization' of problem-solving techniques (p.1-2, p.6, p.8).
domain: competition mathematics (MATH Level 5, seven subjects) (p.3, p.14)
size: 279 original problems, each with a simple and a hard perturbation, so 558 perturbed problems; 164 from the MATH train split and 115 from the test split (p.3); 18 models (p.2, p.5); 12 annotators (p.3)
source_of_items: perturbed from an existing set: hand-written modifications of MATH Level-5 problems by 12 PhD students (p.3)
instances: perturbed (hand-written and static; not generated by code)
has_gold_traces: partial: Figure 3 shows a human-written solution for each perturbed version of its example (p.4), but the paper scores final answers only (p.5)
evaluation: final answer: zero-shot chain of thought, string normalisation and a SymPy equivalence check against the annotated answer; tools disallowed (p.4-5). No step-level scoring. Error analysis by manual inspection of 20 error cases per model (p.6).
human_validation: Items: annotators double-check their own work, an independent annotator cross-validates each modified problem's answer, annotations that failed the checks were removed, and the authors manually went through every problem where o1-mini's answer differed from the annotated answer and confirmed the annotation (p.3). Evaluator: not validated beyond this; the memorisation shares rest on manual inspection of 20 error cases each for two models (p.6).
contamination_measures: perturbations (the benchmark's purpose); seed problems from both MATH splits to compare train and test behaviour; a count of answers equal to the original problem's answer (p.3, p.5-7)

engtrace_use.sentence: Functional, symbolic and perturbed variants of existing problems test whether a model has memorised the original instance (Srivastava et al., 2024; Mirzadeh et al., 2025; Gulati et al., 2025; Huang et al., 2025) [...]
engtrace_use.explanation: The motivation fits: the abstract starts from the question whether performance reflects 'true reasoning capability or memorization' (p.1), and the minimal-edit, changed-answer design is meant to 'elicit potential memorization behaviors' and keep models from 'outputting memorized solutions' (p.3). But the paper's results do not show that its variants test memorisation of the original instance, and the sentence fits MATH-P-Hard worst. (a) MATH-P-Hard changes the problem so the original steps do not apply and 'requires deeper math understanding and harder problem-solving skills' (p.3); the authors say its lower scores 'indicate MATH-P-Hard is more difficult' (p.5), so a drop mixes difficulty with memorisation. (b) The memorisation the paper reports is of techniques, not of the instance: the model 'memorizes the problem-solving techniques from the training set and blindly applies them' (p.2, p.8); the shares (40% of o1-mini's errors, 25% of Claude-3.5-Sonnet's) come from manual inspection of 20 error cases each (p.6). (c) Instance-level recall is checked only by counting answers equal to the original's: under 10% of errors for most models, and 'naive recitation of the training material is not the major reason' (p.6-7). (d) MATH-P-Simple, the instance-level control, shows small drops: most models lose little against the originals, the drops 'mainly come from the train split', test-split accuracies are close to the originals (p.5), and the authors find none of the 58-80% gaps that Srivastava et al. report, 'a sign of the progress in the robustness' (p.5). The sentence is fair for MATH-P-Simple and for the paper's aim, loose for MATH-P-Hard, which the paper itself presents as going beyond the simple perturbations of earlier work that keep the solution pattern (p.1-2, p.8).

suggested_wording: Hand-written hard perturbations of MATH problems, which change the solution method while keeping the text close, lower the accuracy of all 18 models tested, and the authors trace many of the errors to models applying memorised techniques where they no longer fit (Huang et al., 2025).
facts_to_cite: 279 pairs from MATH Level-5 problems (164 from the train split, 115 from the test split), seven subjects (p.3, p.14)
12 PhD-student annotators; each answer cross-validated by an independent annotator; every o1-mini disagreement checked (p.3)
simple perturbation = non-essential change, same solution method, mostly numerical; hard perturbation = small but fundamental change that makes the original method inapplicable (p.3-4)
minimal edits and a changed answer are required for both; embedding retrieval finds the original from the perturbed problem with MRR 0.995 (simple) and 0.986 (hard) (p.3-4)
Table 1: o1-mini 94.27 original, 94.98 simple, 78.49 hard; gemini-2.0-flash-thinking-exp 92.47, 91.04, 78.14 (p.5)
the authors identify 'a new form of memorization': the model memorizes problem-solving techniques and blindly applies them where they no longer suit (p.1-2, p.8)
memorisation accounts for 40% of o1-mini's errors and 25% of Claude-3.5-Sonnet's, from 20 manually inspected error cases each (p.6)
answers equal to the original problem's answer are under 10% of errors for most models; verbatim recitation is not the main reason (p.6-7)
giving the original problem and solution as an in-context example improves MATH-P-Hard by under 5% for most models, because it also misleads (p.7)
MATH-P-Simple drops are small and mainly on the train split; no 58-80% gaps as in Srivastava et al. (p.5)
overlap_with_engtrace: Shares: perturbing existing problems to probe robustness and memorisation, with human annotators checking the answers. Lacks: generated instances (hand-written, static, 279 pairs), any step-level scoring, gold traces used for scoring, an engineering domain (competition mathematics) and a validated scorer. The positioning claim still holds. EngTrace differs in producing variants from code and a private seed, so no annotator is needed to make a variant, and in checking intermediate values rather than the final answer alone.
notes: (1) The abstract's drops (o1-mini -16.49%, gemini-2.0-flash-thinking -12.9%) are MATH-P-Hard against MATH-P-Simple (94.98 - 78.49 and 91.04 - 78.14), not against the original problems (94.27 and 92.47) (p.1, p.5); quote them as drops from the simple version. (2) The instance-memorisation claim in this literature belongs to Srivastava et al.: this paper says they 'created Functional-MATH by manually rewriting the original problems ... into problem templates' and that models are 'biased towards the original configurations of numerical values due to some form of data contamination' (p.1). (3) Venue: the text carries only the arXiv stamp, so the venue named in the brief (ICML 2025) is not confirmable from the text. (4) Case III in appendix C.1: under 10% of problems are solved in the hard version but not in the easier ones, which the authors put down to annotators' difficulty judgements differing from the models' (p.15).
